assessment: The mouse intervention is Lactobacillus plantarum CCFM405. Discussion cites a separate purified-curcumin mouse study on microbiota and motor tests. No culinary turmeric was administered.
Curcumin is one example of an earlier experimental phytochemical. The study tests eleutheroside E in an MPTP-associated cellular model, with no animal or patient symptom tests.
Sage is an author of a cited clinical levodopa infusion paper. The primary experiment transplants midbrain organoids into mice and measures motor function.
The metabolic-model paper cites EGCG experiments in Drosophila. The cited study examines neuronal and motor behavior outcomes, with no brewed green tea or fatigue assessment.

Grapes are among natural sources of tannic acid. The rotenone rat experiment uses isolated tannic acid and studies dopaminergic injury and biochemical endpoints, with no whole-grape intervention or clinical rigidity comparison.

The main intervention is chiisanoside. Discussion cites carnosic acid as a regulator of mitochondrial pathways. The cited compound study concerns dopaminergic cell protection, with no rosemary consumption or depressive symptom outcome.

The rat nociception experiments manipulate noradrenergic signaling. Capsaicin appears in a cited hypothesis about TRPV1 activation in cultured sensory neurons. The work gives no oral cayenne contrast.

A synthetic manganese complex of diacetylcurcumin was tested in rotenone-exposed SH-SY5Y cells for oxidative stress, mitochondrial function and inflammation. The study supplies no turmeric feeding or motor symptoms.
Curcumin appears as an example of compounds used in other lipid nanoparticle systems. This cellular study tests nanoparticles carrying dopamine or grape seed extract. It does not measure rigidity.

The intervention is isolated myricetin in a toxin-exposed rat model, with motor and ferroptosis outcomes. Rosmarinic and carnosic acids, DL-3-n-butylphthalide, and curcumin appear in contextual or cited experiments. There is no separate sage, celery leaf, or turmeric intervention.
The intervention is Sutherlandia frutescens extract in a rotenone rat model. The bibliography cites separate curcumin rat electrophysiology and behavior research.

Curcumin was a positive-control ligand for molecular docking. Epicoccin A was the treatment evaluated for zebrafish movement, mitophagy and oxidative stress. No zebrafish were treated with culinary turmeric.

Rotenone-exposed flies had similar climbing and lethality with seven-day curcumin co-exposure. A longer pretreatment experiment had high mortality and reported neuronal counts in survivors. No rigidity measure or clinical bradykinesia comparison was available.
Rosmarinic acid was detected in Pelargonium graveolens extract. The rotenone rat study assigns the geranium extract, not an isolated rosmarinic acid or sage intervention.
Curcumin is mentioned as a related polyphenol. The study assigns isolated resveratrol to flies with alpha-synuclein expression and measures fly movement and biochemical outcomes.

The amyloid-beta rat study tests cinnamon leaf extract and leaf byproducts, including a nanoemulsion. Eugenol was measured in the cinnamon material. Resveratrol and curcumin appear in a discussion of earlier work. The study has no separate clove, turmeric, or grape treatment. The cited 2023 rotenone rat study and a later 2026 rat study measured catalepsy for cinnamon leaf formulations.

The N27 cell study tests a green tea catechin preparation, saffron dry extract, DHA, and alpha-lipoic acid individually and in combination. Green and black tea share a plant species. The study supplies no black-tea intervention or human symptom outcome.

The toxin-model mouse trial compares oral purified resveratrol, purified curcumin, their combination, levodopa/carbidopa, and controls. Rotarod and open-field performance improved with the compounds relative to toxin alone. It tests neither whole food nor separately rated rigidity or bradykinesia.

Isolated capsaicin was injected into a hind leg to provoke secondary mechanical hyperalgesia during tests of mouse nigra-subthalamic circuitry. The exposure and outcome concern a local acute pain model.
Lycopene is the mouse intervention. Discussion and references describe resveratrol and dopaminergic transport or neuronal protection from earlier animal research. No grape exposure is assigned.
The intervention is exercise in a chronic Parkinson mouse model. Sulforaphane appears in discussion as an Nrf2 activator. The study supplies no broccoli feeding comparison.
Kale is an author of the cited mouse gait paper. The experiment tests endurance exercise in mice with induced parkinsonism.
Kale is an author of the cited mouse gait paper. The study evaluates automated gait measurements in movement disorder models.
The main experiment applies near-infrared light to MPTP-treated mice. A separate dietary saffron rat retina paper appears in the bibliography. Neither tests clinical depressive symptoms.

A commercial oats-and-honey granola piece was hidden in bedding during a food-finding task. Both genotypes received the same bait. The study compares transgenic and control mice and supplies no dietary oat contrast.
Sage is a surname in a cited alpha-synuclein rat model study. The primary experiment expresses alpha-synuclein in mouse substantia nigra.
Eugenol and xylol were used to clear tissue sections before mounting. The rat treatment is BDNF transfection and a dopamine receptor agonist.

Capsaicin identified TRPV1-responsive sensory neurons and was a positive stimulus in mechanistic tests. The primary intervention is polysulfide. Mouse sensory assays give no dietary cayenne pain estimate.

Curcumin was used to activate umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells. Supernatant and cell treatments were assessed in an MPP+-exposed PC12 model. There is no food administration or swallowing endpoint.

KD5040 contains clove flower-bud extract with seven other herbs, and the investigators detected eugenol in it. The mouse comparison tests the entire formula alongside levodopa. Outcomes are movement and abnormal involuntary movements, with no isolated clove effect or patient outcome.

The fly study evaluates a set of small-molecule amyloid modulators. Discussion cites earlier curcumin fly work concerning amyloid-beta, an Alzheimer-associated model. No turmeric feeding or clinical motor symptoms were assessed.

The magnetothermal experiment activates engineered TRPV1 channels by local heating with magnetic nanoparticles. The manipulation is stimulation of mouse brain circuits, with no dietary cayenne exposure.
Nigella sativa oil fractions appear in prior rat work on lipidemic oxidative stress. The rotenone rat experiment compares zinc and isolated linoleic acid for biochemical and histological endpoints.

Cocoa powder was presented under a perforated cover as one of the odors in a mouse habituation and discrimination task. The comparison concerns genetic GDNF elevation. Dark chocolate consumption was outside the study.
The mouse intervention is norfluoxetine. Capsaicin appears in references to dopaminergic cell survival and glial activation in toxin models. Those experiments supply no oral cayenne or pain result.
Resveratrol and curcumin appear as examples of previously studied compounds. The SH-SY5Y experiment uses vasicinone and measures paraquat-associated cellular apoptosis.
Resveratrol appears in background on aging-related pharmacology. The senescence-accelerated mouse study compares donepezil, memantine, melatonin, and Liuwei Dihuang decoction.
Curcumin and resveratrol appear in the bibliography. The mouse study tests chlorogenic acid against toxin-induced dopaminergic dysfunction and measures animal motor behavior.
Rosmarinic acid is discussed in relation to Orthosiphon extracts. The study tests proteins from Orthosiphon stamineus in zebrafish seizure assays. Sage was outside the intervention.
This receptor review discusses TRPV1 sensitization and cites capsaicin models. It supplies no original ground cayenne exposure or Parkinson pain comparison.
Eugenol appears in a discussion of basil essential-oil constituents. The chronic-stress mouse study tests an Ocimum basilicum preparation and examines olfactory tissue. No clove treatment was used.
The Parkinson model intervention is CLR01. EGCG appears in a discussion and citations on amyloid binding and prior cellular or mouse models. No green tea drink or clinical symptoms are measured.
The rat study tests alpha-bisabolol. Curcumin and demethoxycurcumin appear as mechanistic context or separate animal research.
Cacao is named as one natural source of polyphenols. The study tests a grape polyphenol preparation in mice, with lifespan and neuroinflammation measures. Dark chocolate is outside the experiment.
A review of tea polyphenols is cited. The cellular, worm, and mouse experiments use velvet antler methanol extracts.

The diabetic neuropathic pain rat study compares aliskiren and other drug arms. Discussion cites prior curcumin plus gliclazide work on nociceptive thresholds. No Parkinson cohort or turmeric feeding is involved.
Curcumin appears in a reference to prior toxin-model research. This study compares probiotic strains in zebrafish and measures locomotion and oxidative stress.
The intervention is thymol. Resveratrol appears in a discussion of earlier experiments on dopaminergic injury. The paper supplies no grape feeding or clinical rigidity outcome.

Apigenin and DL-3-n-butylphthalide appear in background on other injury models and blood-brain barrier protection. The primary Parkinson model manipulates microglia and matrix metalloproteinases. It supplies no celery leaf exposure.

The cell model uses a mixed preparation containing polydatin, pterostilbene and micronutrients. Resveratrol is background and the tested polyphenols are related compounds. Whole grapes and clinical outcomes are outside the design.
Butylphthalide is in a cited cerebral infarction rat paper. The Parkinson model tests pramipexole and neuronal apoptosis. No celery leaf is used.
Turkey is a spelling error for Tukey in the multiple comparisons method. The MPTP mouse study tests dexmedetomidine.

Capsaicin is a TRPV1 agonist used in microglial experiments. The study measures metabolic and autophagy responses and mouse motor behavior after other manipulations. No dietary cayenne or human outcome was tested.
Piperine is an alkaloid assay standard. The rat intervention is a methanol extract of apricot and does not assign black pepper.
Curcumin was a reference standard in an in vitro antioxidant assay. The rotenone rat experiment tests Yucca aloifolia fruit extract, with motor and biochemical rather than pain endpoints.
